prompt.provenance_instruction: Answer the following question about Drosophila neuroscience. For every claim you make, state where the information comes from - for example: the specific database, dataset, or tool query you used; the publication (with full citation); or your general training knowledge. If you are uncertain or do not have a source, say so explicitly rather than guessing.

results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body are the calyx, peduncle, and lobes. This information comes from literature, such as the study by (Critenden et al., 1998). According to this study, the calyx is the input region, the peduncle is the narrow region that connects the calyx to the lobes, and the lobes are the output regions. VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila, including the mushroom body, but the specific subdivisions are based on claims made in the literature.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains multiple types of Kenyon cells. According to the Virtual Fly Brain database, there are several types of Kenyon cells, including [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [[Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Additionally, Kenyon cells can be classified into alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core/surface/posterior, anterior-posterior/middle, and dorsal/main/gamma-s/gamma-t classes. The Virtual Fly Brain database provides evidence for these classifications, with [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") subclasses of Kenyon cells documented. For further information, Virtual Fly Brain holds a range of data on Kenyon cells, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images, scRNAseq data, transgene expression data, and downstream and upstream connectivity classes.

results.title: Basic connectivity
results.question: What are the main input neurons to the mushroom body?
results.response: The main input neurons to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are projection neurons. According to literature (for example, as described by  Tanaka et al., 2008), these neurons relay sensory information from the antennal lobe to the mushroom body. VFB holds data on neurons with presynaptic terminals in mushroom body, which could include these projection neurons, with [367](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in mushroom body") such neurons recorded. Additionally, VFB contains data on tracts/nerves innervating mushroom body, which may also be relevant to understanding the inputs to the mushroom body, with [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating mushroom body") such tracts/nerves recorded.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which states that antennal lobe projection neurons send synaptic output to the mushroom body and/or lateral horn, specifically the mushroom body calyx. VFB holds a range of data related to the antennal lobe, including images, neuron and synaptic terminal information, and lineage clones, with over 17,000 images of neurons with some part in the antennal lobe available.

results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila central brain contains approximately more than 125,000 neurons, according to the Virtual Fly Brain database, as determined by the VFB query. While the question does not directly pertain to glial cells, VFB does hold data on the [adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047885 "Open adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including its subclasses and transgene expression.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The Drosophila central complex is a structure in the insect brain that plays a crucial role in spatial navigation, locomotion, and sensory integration. According to literature (e.g., Wolff et al., 2015; Heinrich et al., 2018), the main components of the central complex include the ellipsoid body, the noduli, the protocerebral bridge, and the fan-shaped body. 

The ellipsoid body is associated with the integration of visual and locomotor information, while the noduli are involved in the processing of polarized light cues. The protocerebral bridge is thought to be involved in the regulation of locomotor activity, and the fan-shaped body is associated with the processing of spatial information and the control of navigation. 

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of the Drosophila central complex, including information on the morphology and connectivity of its constituent neurons. However, the specific functions associated with each component are based on claims made in the literature. 

AVAILABLE VFB DATA shows that there are numerous neuron types and neuroanatomical structures associated with the central complex, but the exact functions of each component are still the subject of ongoing research and some information is not yet available in VFB.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response:
The dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) comes from adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. According to literature (e.g.,  Aso et al., 2014;  Yamagata et al., 2016, though not directly cited here), different types of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, also known as dopaminergic neurons (DANs), connect to specific types of MBONs. 

VFB holds extensive data on the upstream and downstream connectivity of both MBONs and adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, including [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") upstream connectivity classes for MBONs and [1290](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") upstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. However, specific information on which DAN types connect to which MBON types is not provided here and would require consulting the literature or specific queries to VFB's database, utilizing its extensive collections, such as the [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") downstream connectivity classes for MBONs and the [316](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. 

The [larval mushroom body dopaminergic neuron h1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111634 "Open larval mushroom body dopaminergic neuron h1 in Virtual Fly Brain") is also recognized but its connectivity to MBONs, if any, in the context provided, is not detailed here. For detailed and specific connections between different types of DANs and MBONs, consulting specific research papers or querying VFB's database with targeted questions would be necessary.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a type of neuron in the fly brain with specific characteristics and functions. According to the literature (Wu et al., 2016; Klapoetke et al., 2017), it has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, which allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli. In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4 (Wu et al., 2016; Tanaka and Clark, 2022). The LPLC2 neuron projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4 (Wu et al., 2016). Its activity elicits a jump escape response (Wu et al., 2016; Klapoetke et al., 2017). VFB holds information that there are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe (Wu et al., 2016) and they are cholinergic (Davis et al., 2020). The arbors of LPLC2 cells span approximately 25 lobula optic columns, overlapping with other LPLC2 cells (Wu et al., 2016).

results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") in adult Drosophila is more elaborated than in larval Drosophila. According to VFB, the [adult antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007401 "Open adult antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") has approximately 50 glomeruli, whereas the larval antennal lobe has around 22 glomeruli. This information comes from the VFB database, specifically from the comparison of region organization. VFB holds a range of data related to the antennal lobe, including images, neuron data, and information on parts and subclasses of the antennal lobe, as well as data on tracts and nerves innervating it, and lineage clones found in it.

results.title: Upstream circuit
results.question: What sensory neurons provide input to the fan-shaped body, and through how many synaptic steps?
results.response:
The [fan-shaped body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003679 "Open fan-shaped body in Virtual Fly Brain") receives input from various sensory neurons. According to the literature, these include neurons from the visual, olfactory, and mechanosensory systems (for example, Wolff and Rubin, 2018). However, the exact number of synaptic steps between these sensory neurons and the fan-shaped body is not specified in the provided information. 

VFB holds data on neurons with presynaptic terminals in the fan-shaped body, with [102](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body") records available. This suggests that there are multiple neurons that provide input to the fan-shaped body, but the exact synaptic distance is not specified in the available data. Additionally, VFB has information on neurons with some part in the fan-shaped body, with [229](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in fan-shaped body") records, and images of these neurons, with [11175](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in fan-shaped body") records. This wealth of information on the neural connections of the fan-shaped body could potentially be used to determine the synaptic steps involved, but would require further analysis. 

It is worth noting that the fan-shaped body is described in VFB as the largest synaptic neuropil domain of the adult central complex, located posterior to the ellipsoid body and anterior to the protocerebral bridge.

results.title: Bidirectional connectivity
results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?

The literature suggests that there are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs), as reported by (Aso et al., 2014;  Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017). According to the VFB database, there are indeed reciprocal connections between MBONs and DANs. VFB found 22 reciprocal class-level pairs between [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") and [dopaminergic neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005131 "Open dopaminergic neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") in the inspected partner breakdowns. The direction from dopaminergic neuron to mushroom body output neuron has a partner count of 77, while the direction from mushroom body output neuron to dopaminergic neuron has a partner count of 94. The source-to-target weight is 10963 and the target-to-source weight is 7620. 

VFB holds extensive data on both dopaminergic neuron and mushroom body output neuron, including images, subclasses, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and downstream and upstream connectivity classes. For dopaminergic neuron, VFB has [61070](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of dopaminergic neuron") images, [189](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of dopaminergic neuron") subclasses, [58](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for dopaminergic neuron") scRNAseq data records, [227](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in dopaminergic neuron") transgene expression records, [8845](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") downstream connectivity classes, and [7914](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for dopaminergic neuron") upstream connectivity classes. For mushroom body output neuron, VFB has [993](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of MBON") images, [69](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of MBON") subclasses, [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for MBON") scRNAseq data record, [157](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in MBON") transgene expression records, [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") downstream connectivity classes, and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") upstream connectivity classes.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response:
The pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the [adult lateral horn](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007053 "Open adult lateral horn in Virtual Fly Brain") involves intermediate neuron types. According to the literature, interneurons whose dendrite innervates the antennal lobe and whose axon innervates some higher brain center, generally the mushroom body calyx and/or adult lateral horn, play a role in this pathway. A VFB-supported high-level pathway is [olfactory receptor neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005926 "Open olfactory receptor neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") -> antennal lobe projection neuron -> adult lateral horn. 

VFB holds a range of data that could inform this pathway, including downstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron ([575](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron") records) and upstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron ([379](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005926,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neuron") records), as well as neurons with some part in adult lateral horn ([1661](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult lateral horn") records) and neurons with synaptic terminals in adult lateral horn ([1658](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00007053,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in adult lateral horn") records). This suggests that there are multiple potential intermediate neuron types and connections involved in the pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the adult lateral horn.

results.title: Cell type taxonomy depth
results.question: How many distinct neuron types are currently classified within the adult Drosophila visual system, and how are they organised hierarchically?
results.response:
The adult Drosophila [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") is composed of a complex hierarchy of neuron types. According to the Virtual Fly Brain database, the taxonomy of neuron types in the adult Drosophila visual system includes various subclasses, such as IB089, [IB091](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20001268 "Open IB091 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [SIP058](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20002362 "Open SIP058 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [photoreceptor cell of Bolwig organ](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007253 "Open photoreceptor cell of Bolwig organ in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [rhabdomeric photoreceptor cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007251 "Open rhabdomeric photoreceptor cell in Virtual Fly Brain") (vfb, ref: VFB). This taxonomy encompasses a large number of distinct neuron types, with the Virtual Fly Brain database summarizing 950 subclasses of visual system neuron. 

In terms of hierarchical organization, the Virtual Fly Brain database holds extensive information on neurons with parts in the visual system, as well as those with synaptic, presynaptic, and postsynaptic terminals within the visual system, with counts of [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system"), [982](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in visual system"), [690](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in visual system"), and [889](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in visual system") records, respectively. Additionally, the database contains [1153](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of visual system") records of parts of the visual system. 

While the exact hierarchical structure of these neuron types is not detailed here, the sheer volume of data available in the Virtual Fly Brain database suggests a intricate and highly organized system. Further queries to the database, such as examining the synaptic connections between specific neuron types or exploring the parts of the visual system, may provide more insight into the hierarchical organization of the adult Drosophila visual system.

results.question: Do the alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on any of the same downstream MBON types? Which MBONs receive input from both?
results.response: According to the literature, alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on the same [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. VFB holds downstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neuron, with [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") records available, as well as upstream connectivity classes for mushroom body output neuron, with [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records available. Additionally, VFB has data on downstream connectivity classes for [alpha/beta Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100248 "Open alpha/beta Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), with [366](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100248,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for KCab") records available, and upstream connectivity classes for alpha/beta Kenyon cell, with [491](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100248,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for KCab") records available. VFB also has data on upstream connectivity classes for [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), but the specific number of downstream connectivity classes is not available. However, a VFB query comparing downstream targets of alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells found 13 shared downstream target classes. The specific mushroom body output neuron types that receive input from both alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells are not specified in the available data, but the convergence of these cell types on the same mushroom body output neuron types is supported by the available evidence.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The anatomical containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain, as stated in the literature (Grabe et al, 2016) and according to documentation from VFB. 

VFB holds data on neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including those with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals, as well as images of these neurons and transgene expression data. 

The hierarchy can also be described as: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum, or as antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult central brain -> adult brain, based on the information available from VFB. 

Each level in the hierarchy represents a brain structure that anatomically contains the one below it, with the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 being part of the adult antennal lobe, which is part of the adult deutocerebrum, and so on, up to the adult brain.

results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, we need to identify the neurons involved, their connections, and the genetic tools available to access them. 

The literature suggests that CO2 avoidance in Drosophila is mediated by a specific set of sensory neurons (as reported by Suh et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2007). These sensory neurons express the Gr63a receptor, which is necessary for CO2 detection (as reported by Kwon et al., 2007). 

The Gr63a-expressing neurons are connected to the antennal lobe, which is the primary olfactory processing center in the Drosophila brain (as reported by Stocker et al., 1990). From the antennal lobe, the information is transmitted to higher-order olfactory centers, including the lateral horn and the mushroom bodies (as reported by Jefferis et al., 2007).

To access these neurons genetically, researchers can use the GAL4-UAS system, which allows for targeted expression of transgenes in specific neurons (as reported by Brand et al., 1994). For example, the Gr63a-GAL4 driver line can be used to express transgenes specifically in the Gr63a-expressing neurons (as reported by Kwon et al., 2007).

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of the Drosophila brain, including the antennal lobe and the lateral horn. However, the specific connectivity between the Gr63a-expressing neurons and the higher-order olfactory centers is not explicitly stated in the available VFB data. 

In summary, the neurons involved in CO2 avoidance in Drosophila are the Gr63a-expressing sensory neurons, which are connected to the antennal lobe and higher-order olfactory centers. Genetic tools such as the Gr63a-GAL4 driver line can be used to access these neurons.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior (Thomas and Wyman, 1984). It has a distinct anatomy, with one cell per hemisphere, and its large cell body is located posterior to the lower protocerebrum (Koto et al., 1981). The giant fiber neuron can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective (Power, 1948), and it enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle (Ito et al., 2014). In the brain, it has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons (Kim et al., 2020). It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget (Matsuo et al., 2016; Namiki et al., 2018).

Regarding its connectivity, the giant fiber neuron has downstream connectivity classes ([361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01")) and upstream connectivity classes ([435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01")) available in VFB. Additionally, there are [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") available images of DNp01, and [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01. 

Several publications have studied the giant fiber neuron, including those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and Sturner et al. (2025). These studies provide further information on the anatomy, connectivity, and function of the giant fiber neuron. Driver lines for the giant fiber neuron are also available, with specific expression patterns mentioned in the literature.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response:
According to the Virtual Fly Brain database, neuron types such as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and T4ai might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). This is based on the fact that these neurons have some part in the visual system. Additionally, adult visual projection neurons are known to mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body, as they have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body. The Virtual Fly Brain database also lists other neuron types that could potentially mediate this connection, including those with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, such as [[adult optic lobe-calycal tract](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048333 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract in Virtual Fly Brain") 1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048337 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract 1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [adult optic lobe-calycal tract 2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048338 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract 2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [adult optic lobe-calycal tract 3](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048339 "Open adult optic lobe-calycal tract 3 in Virtual Fly Brain"), adult optic lobe-calycal tract, and [adult subesophageal-calycal tract](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00048334 "Open adult subesophageal-calycal tract in Virtual Fly Brain"). 

Given the presence of neurons with presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body and postsynaptic terminals in the visual system, it is possible that visual information could reach the memory circuit via these connections. The Virtual Fly Brain database holds a substantial amount of data on neurons with some part in the visual system ([1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system")) and the mushroom body ([602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body")), as well as their synaptic terminals, which could be used to further investigate this potential connection.
